steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction to our paper on rescaling PCA maps with mutual information, applied to genetic distance. It should lay out the problem with correlation as a measure of information distance, include a subsection on information and correlation (how experts misread nonlinear metrics, why entropy methods help, relevance to genetics and existing criticisms of PCA), and end with how the rest of the paper is organized.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Even if we assume that two variables X and Y are both normally distributed (or, more generally, in the class with rapid convergence to the normal, or "thin tailed", thanks to the approximative behavior), the correlation between them does not adequately reflect the information distance between them. Squared correlation would not do it either. The distortion becomes acute with Principal Component Analysis, PCA, and the genetic two-dimensional maps, where there is a built-in correlation component.

For example, if we correlate 2 vectors X_{1} and X_{2} against Y (taking Y as the basis), the information does not scale linearly, even though correlation reflects a measure of the noise in a linear dependence. So the correlation metric needs some kind of scaling. A .5 correlation is vastly and disproportionally inferior to, say, .7.

## I-A Information and correlation

Experts have been shown to be misled by nonlinear metrics, hence the need to "linearize" whatever metric is used. There are perceptual constraints, compounded by the nonlinearity of the measure. For instance, Soyer et al showed that a great many econometricians, who are well-versed statisticians, almost always overlook the real inferential and practical implications, and all the interpretation errors go in one direction, the fooled by randomness one (i.e. underestimating the noise). That 70 pct. of econometricians misinterpreted their own results says a lot. The corresponding author has documented a version of the effect: professionals and graduate students did not realize that they interpreted mean deviation as standard deviation, so they underestimated volatility, especially under non-Normality. It has also been shown that correlation is not additive across subsections of the domain under consideration, even when the variables are Gaussian.

The only cure, since the evidence is strong that the level of statistical education doesn't help, is to avoid presenting nonlinear measures and to linearize whatever is presented to the specialist before the scientific implication. Entropy methods are additive, unlike correlation, so they solve the problem.

- ML / genetics
  - ML loss functions use cross-entropy; DNA is information -> information-theoretic metric preferable
  - mutual information ~ "how much should one dynamically gamble on X knowing Y" -> genetic distance
  - entropy helps scale runs of homozygosity (ROH); phylogenetic attributes PCA used to sort out
- Other criticisms of PCA: sample size mismatch, cherry picking, 2-D insufficiency; fixable with standard checks; ours fundamental
- Organization: MI mapping of PCs (orthogonality heuristic); matrix math for genetics; results on world population and subsample

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Even if we assume that two variables X and Y are both normally distributed (or, more generally, in the class with rapid convergence to the normal, or "thin tailed", thanks to the approximative behavior), the correlation between them does not adequately reflect the information distance between them. So the correlation metric needs some kind of scaling. A .5 correlation is vastly and disproportionally inferior to, say, .7.

## I-A Information and correlation

Experts have been shown to be misled by nonlinear metrics, hence the need to "linearize" whatever metric is used. There are perceptual constraints, compounded by the nonlinearity of the measure. For instance, Soyer et al showed that a great many econometricians, who are well-versed statisticians, almost always overlook the real inferential and practical implications, and all the interpretation errors go in one direction, the fooled by randomness one (i.e. underestimating the noise). That 70 pct. of econometricians misinterpreted their own results says a lot. The corresponding author has documented a version of the effect: professionals and graduate students did not realize that they interpreted mean deviation as standard deviation, so they underestimated volatility, especially under non-Normality. It has also been shown that correlation is not additive across subsections of the domain under consideration, even when the variables are Gaussian.

The only cure, since the evidence is strong that the level of statistical education doesn't help, is to avoid presenting nonlinear measures and to linearize whatever is presented to the specialist before the scientific implication. Entropy methods are additive, unlike correlation, so they solve the problem.

Not every branch of research falls for correlation, which is a relatively uninformational metric. Machine learning loss functions rely on cross-entropy methods. And since DNA is, well, information, an information-theoretic metric would most certainly be preferable to what is currently in standard use.

Also, mutual information maps to "how much should one dynamically gamble on X knowing Y ", so its information-theoretic quality is most applicable to genetic distance. Besides PCA analysis, entropy methods are also helpful for properly scaling runs of homozygosity (ROH), that is, contiguous lengths of homozygous genotypes present in an individual because the parents transmitted identical haplotypes to their offspring. These attributes emerge naturally in the phylogenetic situations that PCA has been used to sort out.

Other criticisms of PC analysis have been made recently. PC has a spate of weaknesses, many related to sample size mismatch, the ability to cherry pick, or the insufficiency of representing things in two dimensions. But these are standard statistical problems, which spread because of flaws in the applications and not because of a fundamental structural problem, and they can be fixed with more rigorous but standard checks. Our approach shows fundamental differences that these conventional checks cannot cure.

The rest of the discussion is organized as follows. First we propose a new way to map PCs using mutual information. This uses a convenient property: since PCA vectors for Gaussian variables are orthogonal both for correlation and for mutual information, we can use a simple heuristic for the translation. Second we give the precise mathematics applied to genetics in matrix form, which maps to our exact implementation on population maps. Finally we show the results for the world population and for a subsample of it, with comments on the significant divergences between the methods.

steps.text:
Correlation between two variables X and Y, even if we assume that both variables are normally distributed (or, more generally, in the class of rapid convergence to the normal, or "thin tailed" thanks to the approximative behavior [1]), does not adequately reflect the information distance between them. Nor does squared correlation. This distortion becomes acute with Principal Component Analysis, PCA, and the genetic two-dimensional maps, where there is a built-in correlation component.

For instance, if we are correlating 2 vectors X_{1} and X_{2} against Y (assuming it is the basis), the information does not scale linearly (even though correlation reflects a measure of the noise in a linear dependence). There must be some scaling of the correlation metric. A .5 correlation is vastly and disproportionally inferior to, say, .7.

## I-A Information and correlation

It has been shown that experts can be misled by nonlinear metrics, hence the need to "linearize" whatever metric is used. Perceptual constraints are compounded by the nonlinearity of the measure; for instance, Soyer et al [2] showed how a great many econometricians, who are well-versed statisticians, almost always overlook the real inferential and practical implications, and all interpretation errors go in one direction, the fooled by randomness one (i.e. underestimation of noise). That 70 pct. of econometricians misinterpreted their own results is quite telling. The corresponding author has documented a version of the effect in [3]: professionals and graduate students failed to realize that they interpreted mean deviation as standard deviation, thereby underestimating volatility, especially under non-Normality. It has also been shown in [4] that correlation is not additive across subsections of the domain under consideration, even when the variables are Gaussian.

The only cure (the evidence is strong that the level of statistical education doesn't help) is to avoid presenting nonlinear measures and to linearize whatever is presented to the specialist before the scientific implication. Entropy methods, being additive (unlike correlation), solve the problem.

Not all branches of research fall for correlation as a relatively uninformational metric. Machine learning loss functions rely on cross-entropy methods [5]. Since DNA is, well, information, an information-theoretic metric would most certainly be preferable to what is in current standard use.

Further, since mutual information maps to "how much should one dynamically gamble on X knowing Y ", its information-theoretic quality is most applicable to genetic distance. In addition to PCA analysis, entropy methods are helpful to properly scale runs of homozygosity (ROH) (that is, contiguous lengths of homozygous genotypes present in an individual due to parents transmitting identical haplotypes to their offspring). These attributes emerge naturally in phylogenetic situations that PCA has been used to sort out [6].

Other criticisms of PC analysis have recently been made: PC has a spate of weaknesses, many of which relate to sample size mismatch, the ability to perform cherry picking, or the insufficiency of representation in two dimensions, as reported in [7]. However, these are standard statistical problems, spreading because of flaws in the applications rather than a fundamental structural problem, and are fixable with more rigorous but standard checks. Our approach shows fundamental differences not curable by these conventional checks.

The rest of this discussion is organized as follows. First, we propose a new way to map PCs using mutual information, thanks to a convenient property: because PCA vectors for Gaussian variables are orthogonal both for correlation and for mutual information, we can apply a simple heuristic for the translation. Second, we express the precise mathematics applied to genetics in matrix form, mapping to our exact implementation on population maps. Finally, we show the results as applied to the world population, as well as a subsample of it, with comments on the significant divergences between methods.

[2] E. Soyer and R. M. Hogarth, “The illusion of predictability: How regression statistics mislead experts,” International Journal of Forecasting , vol. 28, no. 3, pp. 695–711, 2012.
